pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Identify different labelled samples of rocks presented in the classroom or laboratory.
- Describe the visible characteristics of each rock.
- Collect samples of rocks from around the community, label them using a rock identification guide, and compare them with labelled laboratory samples.
- Research and report the stages of weathering of rocks to form soil.

pages.title: Rocks as the Origin of Soil
pages.body: All soil ultimately originates from rock that has been broken down over long periods of time through a process called weathering. Igneous rock, sedimentary rock and metamorphic rock are the three main types of rock found on earth, and understanding their differences helps explain why soils in different areas can have different physical properties, since the type of parent rock strongly influences the type of soil that eventually forms above it.

lessons.title: The Three Main Types of Rock

pages.title: The Three Main Types of Rock
pages.body:
How each rock forms, and its visible characteristics, are two useful ways to identify and distinguish igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rock, as summarised in the table below.

| **ROCK TYPE** | **HOW IT FORMS** | **VISIBLE CHARACTERISTICS** |
|---|---|---|
| **Igneous rock** | Forms when hot, molten rock (magma or lava) cools and hardens | Often hard, with visible crystals, for example granite |
| **Sedimentary rock** | Forms when layers of sediment, such as sand or mud, are compressed over time | Often shows visible layers, for example sandstone |
| **Metamorphic rock** | Forms when existing rock is changed by heat and pressure over time | Often has a banded or layered appearance, for example marble or slate |

pages.title: Stages of Weathering, from Rock to Soil
pages.body:
Exposure, physical breakdown, chemical breakdown, and mixing with organic matter are four general stages describing how solid rock is gradually transformed into soil over time.

- First, rock becomes exposed at or near the earth's surface, where it is affected by rain, wind, sunlight and temperature changes.

- Second, physical weathering breaks the rock into smaller fragments, for example through repeated expansion and contraction caused by heating during the day and cooling at night, or through the force of plant roots growing into cracks.

- Third, chemical weathering further breaks down the minerals within these rock fragments, for example through reactions with rainwater, gradually turning hard rock fragments into finer particles.

- Fourth, these fine mineral particles mix with decayed plant and animal matter, known as humus, eventually forming the layered, fertile material we recognise as soil.

11.4  Practical Illustration

[[img:icb63f0a9b|]]

Fig 11.1  The stages of weathering, showing how solid rock gradually breaks down to form soil

Notice how each stage produces progressively smaller and finer material, moving from a single large rock, to cracked rock, to small fragments, and finally to soil. This process typically takes an extremely long time, often many thousands of years, which is one reason soil is considered a valuable, slowly renewable resource that must be protected from erosion and degradation.

lessons.title: Examples and Uses of the Three Types of Rock

pages.title: Examples and Uses of the Three Types of Rock
pages.body:
| **ROCK TYPE** | **EXAMPLES** | **USES** |
|---|---|---|
| **Igneous** | Granite, basalt, pumice | Granite is crushed into chippings for roads and buildings. Pumice is used for scrubbing |
| **Sedimentary** | Sandstone, limestone, shale | Limestone is used to make cement. Sandstone is used for building. Coal, crude oil and natural gas are found in sedimentary rocks, and many contain fossils |
| **Metamorphic** | Marble, which forms from limestone. Slate, which forms from shale. Gneiss, which forms from granite | Marble is used for floor tiles and statues. Slate is used for roofing and floor tiles |

pages.title: Types of Weathering
pages.body:
| **TYPE** | **WHAT CAUSES IT** | **EXAMPLE** |
|---|---|---|
| **Physical weathering** | Heating and cooling, running water and wind break rock into smaller pieces without changing what it is made of | Rocks crack after being heated by day and cooled at night for many years |
| **Chemical weathering** | Rainwater, which is slightly acidic, and oxygen react with the minerals in rock and change them | Limestone slowly dissolves in rainwater, and rocks that contain iron turn reddish brown |
| **Biological weathering** | Living things break up rock | Tree roots widen cracks, burrowing animals loosen rock, and lichens release acids onto rock |

Rocks change slowly from one type to another in a rock cycle. Igneous rock is weathered into sediments, which harden into sedimentary rock. Heat and pressure change sedimentary or igneous rock into metamorphic rock. Rock that melts deep in the earth forms magma, which cools to form new igneous rock.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Different parent rocks tend to produce different soil characteristics. For example, areas with granite, an igneous rock, often develop sandy, well drained soils, while areas with certain sedimentary rocks may develop soils with more clay content. This connection between rock type and resulting soil type is one reason soil properties can vary noticeably even between neighbouring areas with different underlying geology.
